Today the channels import the bwrap composer directly (sidecar.py:316, local_channel.py:25), bootstrap hard-imports WslConnector (runtime.py:139) and the layout grammar (runtime.py:727/739/784), the coordinator is never called on the product path, the sandbox never declares isolation.wrap@1 while preflight treats an undeclared capability as passing, and legacy_codex.py is dead code that would re-fuse the layers if revived. This order consumes the existing protocol (MountPlan -> wrap -> IsolatedProcessSpec), unifies the two capability vocabularies and makes an undeclared capability a refusal, moves the layout grammar into the contracts layer, registers the wsl host provider, adds a sandbox conformance gate whose counter-example must fail, and keeps behaviour byte-identical (the substitution gate and the four family gates stay green). orders.note: Native Windows placement: Server on Windows, harness on Windows, AppContainer as the sandbox (capability based, access granted by ACL, no virtualisation so the home stays a real directory), a Job Object for the tree and its lifetime, and no Worker at all because the Server already runs on that machine and reads the directory directly for the audit. Materialisation has no bind mount to lean on, so config goes to a per-execution directory pointed at by environment variables (or into the home with an ACL granting read only, when a harness insists on a fixed filename), credentials go into the child's environment block, and the tmpfs masks become 'do not write plus delete', never recorded as masked. Read isolation is the linchpin: the official wording is that read-only access is less restricted, so it must be measured, and if reads are not denied the capability is declared false and the platform is reported as weaker than Linux. Wasted: Windows Sandbox (VM shape, mapped folders are a redirected filesystem), Windows containers, Sandboxie, minifilters, and remapping (junctions or a per-process DOS device) except when a harness hardcodes a path.

orders.note: Subscriptions become a credential kind beside api-key, but the login state is NOT kept in the native home: it is a managed asset in the control plane (encrypted in the SecretStore), materialised into the profile home per turn as a writable working copy and reclaimed at the end, which makes hot switching fall out for free - the next turn is a fresh process reading a freshly materialised home, so changing the bound account needs no CLI restart. This introduces the first write-back path in the product, so it is bounded and explicit: only the declared files are reclaimed, over-limit is a typed failure that keeps the previous asset, one lock per account serialises concurrent turns, a lost lock is a typed conflict rather than a silent overwrite, and writes are atomic with the digest recorded. Tokens never reach logs, argv, events or evidence; the host's own login state is never read; nothing is filled in or scraped. Stage A must establish per family where the login state lives, whether it is a single file, whether it is machine bound, and whether the harness rewrites it - any family that fails one of those is declared unsupported for subscriptions rather than faked. Order 45's credential scan matches only the injected per-run value, so the materialised working copy is not a leak, and that note goes into code and tests.

orders.note: Harness programs become product objects: an installed set per family (version, tree digest, source, size, entry count, install time), a catalog of available versions synced into the control plane so the UI paints immediately, and install, update and rollback as explicit user actions. Versions live in content-addressed directories with the active one held as a reference, so updating adds a directory and moves the reference - running sessions are unaffected and rollback is just moving it back. Fetches and builds happen on the execution side, bounded and cancellable, and the tree digest is always re-derived; a signature is verified when one exists and the weaker 'digest pinned only' fact is recorded when it does not. No automatic updates, no silent source switching, failures never land (atomic replacement keeps the previous version), and the profile home's cross-version compatibility stays the harness's business but must be reported honestly rather than papered over. The references were gathered this round: Applite's catalog-first, asynchronously annotated package UI is the reusable pattern, Ollama's repository tree hints at version-pin plus manifest plus content-addressed blobs without documenting it, and two negatives matter as much - claude-squad makes users update the CLI themselves and vibe-kanban assumes installed agents and is sunsetting, so this class has no existing implementation to copy. Stage A must establish per family which official source exists, whether it is signed, and whether the harness self-updates, since a self-updating harness has to be handled by treating our installed tree as authoritative.

orders.note: Hooks are three different kinds of thing and this order refuses to flatten them: Claude Code is declarative (event to matcher group to handlers, with a large event catalog, five handler types, per-event timeouts, stdin JSON in and exit-code plus JSON out, and a read-only /hooks menu of its own); Codex exposes only a managed-hooks-only switch in the documentation reachable this round, so stage A must establish its event model by observation; OpenCode hooks are JS/TS plugins that mutate input/output and can register tools, which is code rather than configuration, so they are treated as code assets the user supplies with a digest and a preview instead of being assembled from form fields. One UI shell, per-family models validated against a declared schema, materialised into the read-only projection the harness already receives, with a typed refusal for an event the family does not support. Hooks stay disabled until the user enables them and can see the full command; they run inside the sandbox with that execution's isolation and network posture; trigger facts (id, event, time, exit code, bounded output summary) land in the ledger, and a blocking exit code is reported as blocking rather than as an ordinary success.

Resolution may only ever tighten what a tool could already do. Two semantic corrections ride along: a session is not owned by a profile - it belongs to the workspace and the product, the profile is the current binding, and attribution is per turn, which the schema already does via server_turns.profile_id, profile_revision and native_generation - and a family is strongly bound to a profile, so switching harness in place is not offered; the only path is cloning into a new profile of another family, copying and translating as much as each family allows, never migrating session-type assets, and never pretending the clone inherited the old native session. Switching the binding within the same harness is allowed and honest per the family's storage shape: file-per-session journals let the session's own native files move into the new home with an auditable record, while shared-database families restart natively and say so.

orders.dependency_condition: Needs the MCP materialisation of 58 and the profile authorisation and permission rules of 60; folds into the same wire relock as 51-64.
orders.note: A profile can call another profile as a subagent through two fixed MCP tools. The contract is copied from the convergent shape of native subagent invocation, established first-hand on 2026-09-17: the majority (Claude Code Task {subagent_type, prompt, description}, OpenCode task {description, prompt, subagent_type, task_id?} in packages/opencode/src/tool/task.ts with its task.txt description template, Roo new_task) is one generic dispatch tool whose description carries the roster, returning the child's single final summary; Cline's per-agent dynamic tools (use_subagent_<sanitized> in SubagentToolName.ts, agents from YAML frontmatter in AgentConfigLoader.ts) are the minority shape and were rejected because the tool table would change with authorisation and descriptions would sit permanently in the parent's prompt. So run_subagent takes subagent, a three-to-five word description and a self-contained prompt, plus optional narrowing knobs; list_subagents gives full detail; the roster digest lives in the tool description so one call suffices, and neither tool is materialised when the authorised edge set is empty. The words ask/ask_profile are dropped: asking for an answer is a different act from dispatching work that runs autonomously and returns a summary. Inheritance follows OpenCode's deriveSubagentSessionPermission: the child inherits the parent's deny rules and external-directory restrictions while its allow set comes from its own profile, and run_subagent is denied by default for a child unless that child's own authorisation grants it, so depth is a default deny rather than only a counter (the per-turn and depth counters stay as a second layer). task_id resumes the same child native session, a handle rather than a profile-owned object, and cross-family resume is a typed refusal that never silently starts a fresh stint. The Server runs the child as a normal execution with its own sandbox, home, model slot and permission rules, so context is not inherited, the child's result is not shown to the user and the parent must relay it, usage and cost roll into the calling turn, approvals surface as interruptions, cancelling the parent cancels the children, and concurrent invocation is supported (at most four per turn) on the same no-clobber guarantee as order 45. Optional parameters may only tighten, a single call is capped at ten minutes, cycles are typed refusals, and authorisation edges are explicit and default empty. Background mode (OpenCode's background=true with completion notification) is explicitly not done because it would need a new event kind and the wire is locked; permission bypass is never a default, the opposite of claude-code-mcp's --dangerously-skip-permissions.
